code.title: CRTP: static polymorphism without a vtable

followUps:
You get a compile error, because the base calls areaImpl() on the derived type and the name is not found. If the derived class inherits some other function of that name from its parent, the base silently calls the wrong one instead.

Example: struct Tri : Shape<Tri> {} with no areaImpl fails inside Shape<Tri>::area. Unlike a pure virtual function, the error shows up only when the call is instantiated. Concepts or static_assert in the base give a clearer message.

Make the base constructor private and declare the derived type a friend, so only the right class can build it.

template <class D> class Base {
    Base() = default;
    friend D;
};
struct A : Base<A> {};   // fine
struct B : Base<A> {};   // error: B cannot reach Base ctor

The mistake is caught at compile time, with no run-time cost.

It removes most reasons for CRTP: a member function can take an explicit object parameter, so the base no longer needs to know the derived type.

struct Base {
    template <class Self>
    void describe(this Self&& self) { self.areaImpl(); }
};
struct Sq : Base { double areaImpl() const; };

Self is deduced as the real type of the object, so there is no template parameter on the class and no static_cast. Simpler to read, and it also lets you forward const and value category.

code.title: Pimpl idiom: incomplete type behind a unique_ptr

followUps:
Because unique_ptr<Impl> needs the full definition of Impl at the point where its deleter is instantiated, and the destructor is where that happens.

If the compiler generates the destructor inline in the header, Impl is still incomplete there, and delete on an incomplete type is a compile error (or silent undefined behavior with a raw pointer). Declare ~Widget(); in the header and write Widget::~Widget() = default; in the .cpp, after Impl is defined. The move operations need the same treatment.

Fast pimpl keeps the Impl object inside the class in aligned raw storage, so there is no heap allocation.

class W {
    alignas(8) unsigned char buf_[64];
    struct Impl; Impl* p() { return reinterpret_cast<Impl*>(buf_); }
};  // .cpp: new (buf_) Impl; static_assert(sizeof(Impl) <= 64);

You pay by hard-coding a size and alignment in the header; the .cpp must static_assert that the real Impl fits. If Impl grows past 64 bytes, the header changes again, which loses part of the ABI benefit.

Usually no: unique_ptr matches the ownership, because each object owns its own Impl exclusively.

shared_ptr would let copies share one Impl, so changing a copy changes the original, which surprises callers. It also adds a control block and atomic reference counts. A rare good use is an immutable Impl shared cheaply between copies (copy-on-write style). One small plus: shared_ptr remembers its deleter, so the destructor can stay defaulted in the header.

code.title: Type erasure: a minimal std::function

followUps:
Because std::function copies and moves the stored callable, and a throwing move would leave the inline buffer half-built with no safe way to recover.

If the callable is stored in a small buffer inside the function object, moving the function means moving the callable byte by byte into the new buffer. When that move can throw, the library could not offer a noexcept move for std::function itself. So implementations only use the buffer when is_nothrow_move_constructible is true; otherwise they allocate on the heap, and moving then just swaps a pointer.

std::function_ref is a non-owning view of a callable: it stores a pointer to the object plus a function pointer, and never copies or allocates.

void each(function_ref<void(int)> f);
int sum = 0;
each([&](int x){ sum += x; });   // lambda lives in caller

It is the right parameter type for callbacks that are only used during the call. It must not be stored beyond the lifetime of the callable. std::function owns its target, so it can be stored, but it may allocate and is costlier.

Because std::function must be copyable, and a lambda holding a unique_ptr is move-only, so the copy operation cannot be generated.

The type-erased wrapper has a virtual clone; building Model<F>::clone would copy the lambda, which copies the unique_ptr, which is deleted, so the constructor fails to compile. Fixes: C++23 std::move_only_function, wrapping the pointer in a shared_ptr, or using a generic template parameter instead.

code.title: Copy-and-swap assignment

followUps:
Because std::swap(*this, other) uses the move constructor and move assignment, and move assignment is usually defined in terms of this very operator, so you get endless recursion.

With operator=(T other) { std::swap(*this, other); } the swap does T tmp(move(a)); a = move(b); b = move(tmp);. The line a = move(b) calls the same operator= again, and the stack overflows. Provide your own member-wise swap (swapping pointer and size), and call it through an unqualified call so ADL finds it.

Not if both take the same kind of argument: operator=(T) and operator=(T&&) make a call like a = T(5) ambiguous, and the compiler rejects it.

The by-value version already covers both cases: lvalues are copied into the parameter, rvalues are moved in. So pick one style. Either use the single by-value operator, or the pair operator=(const T&) and operator=(T&&), which avoids one extra move but needs more code.

Force an allocation failure part-way through, then check that nothing leaked and the object is unchanged.

Steps: (1) replace operator new with one that throws on the Nth call; (2) loop N from 1 up, run the operation, catch bad_alloc; (3) after each failure assert the original value is intact (strong guarantee); (4) run under AddressSanitizer or Valgrind to catch leaks. The loop ends when the operation succeeds with no throw, so every allocation point has been tested.

code.title: Strong vs basic exception guarantee

followUps:
Because vector promises the strong guarantee on growth, and it can only keep that promise if moving elements cannot throw.

When it reallocates, it moves elements to the new block. If a move threw half way, the old elements would already be damaged and could not be restored. So it uses std::move_if_noexcept: a noexcept move is used, otherwise it falls back to copying (if copyable), which is slower. With 1,000,000 strings, a missing noexcept turns cheap moves into 1,000,000 copies.

The single-element insert gives the strong guarantee: if it throws, the map is unchanged.

The node is built first; if the key already exists or an exception occurs, the tree is left as it was. Range insert (insert(first, last)) only gives the basic guarantee, because elements before the failure stay inserted. This is one reason node-based containers are easier to reason about than vector in the middle.

code.title: Scope guard with scope_fail

followUps:
If the cleanup callable throws inside the destructor, the exception escapes a noexcept destructor and the program calls std::terminate.

Destructors are implicitly noexcept, so a throwing cleanup is fatal. Library guards (GSL finally) simply do this. Safer designs wrap the call in try { f(); } catch (...) {} and log, or require the callable to be noexcept with a static_assert(is_nothrow_invocable_v<F>). Cleanup code should not fail anyway.

Because an unnamed temporary is destroyed at the end of the same statement, so the cleanup would run immediately.

ScopeExit(f);        // temporary: f runs right now
ScopeExit guard(f);  // lives until end of scope

The statement ScopeExit(f); may even be parsed as a declaration of a variable named f. This is why libraries provide a macro that creates a uniquely named variable, and why [[nodiscard]] on the class helps catch the mistake.

Start the transaction, then create a scope_fail whose action is rollback; if you reach the end normally, the guard simply does nothing.

db.begin();
scope_fail undo([&]{ db.rollback(); });
db.insert(a);
db.insert(b);   // may throw: rollback runs
db.commit();    // normal path: no rollback

Put the guard right after begin() so that every later throw is covered. Commit must be the last statement, so a failure in commit itself also rolls back.

code.title: Destructors are noexcept: explicit close() instead

followUps:
Inside a destructor you can call std::uncaught_exceptions() and compare it with the value saved at construction: a larger count means the stack is unwinding.

Example: guard created when the count is 0; if later the count is 1 in the destructor, an exception is in flight. The old std::uncaught_exception() returned only a bool and gave wrong answers for objects created during unwinding (it said true even for a nested guard that exited normally). Use this only for scope_fail-style cleanup, not to decide whether it is safe to throw: a destructor should not throw either way.

It catches the error and sets failbit or badbit; no exception leaves the destructor.

The stream's destructor closes the file buffer and swallows anything that goes wrong, so a failed flush can be lost silently. That is the textbook reason to call close() yourself and check fail() (or enable exceptions()) before the object goes out of scope, when losing data matters.

code.title: C++20 generator coroutine

followUps:
Because after the coroutine finishes, the frame should still exist so that the caller can safely ask done() and read the result from the promise.

With suspend_never at the final point, the frame is destroyed automatically as the coroutine ends, and a later h.done() or h.promise() uses freed memory. Suspending at the end keeps the frame alive; the owner then calls destroy() in its destructor. It is also noexcept-friendly: final_suspend must not throw.

Symmetric transfer lets one coroutine hand control straight to another, without growing the call stack: await_suspend returns a coroutine_handle and the compiler resumes it as a tail call.

Without it, a chain of 1,000,000 tasks each resuming the next from inside await_suspend would nest 1,000,000 stack frames and overflow. With it, the depth stays constant. It is how Task types continue the awaiting parent when a child finishes.

Because the coroutine frame outlives the call: the parameter is copied into the frame, but a reference parameter is copied as a reference, which then points to something that may be gone.

Task f(const std::string& s) { co_await later(); use(s); }
f("hi");   // temporary string dies, s dangles

After the first suspend, the caller's temporary is destroyed. Take parameters by value in coroutines, or make sure the referred object outlives every resume.

code.title: Many stackless coroutines in a round-robin

followUps:
Asio's co_spawn starts the coroutine on an executor you give it, and every co_await on an Asio operation resumes the coroutine on that same executor.

The coroutine body runs as a posted handler. When a socket read completes, the completion handler re-posts the resume to the executor, so with a single-threaded io_context all coroutines are interleaved on one thread with no locks. With a strand or a thread pool, resumption follows that executor's rules.

Yes, it can. A coroutine is just a heap frame, so any thread that calls resume() runs it, provided only one thread resumes it at a time.

It may suspend on thread A and be resumed by thread B, for example after an async IO completes in a pool. Pitfalls: thread_local variables and thread-owned locks change meaning after the move, and a mutex held across co_await may be unlocked by a different thread, which is undefined behavior. Use an executor or strand to keep control over where it runs.

code.title: ABI break: layout change moves a member

followUps:
Mostly because of compatibility: changing its layout would break every binary built against it, and the standard's iterator-invalidation and bucket interface rules lock the node-based design in.

The standard requires pointers and references to elements to stay valid after rehash, and exposes the bucket API, which forces separate chaining with one allocation per element. A faster open-addressing table (like Abseil's flat map) breaks those promises. Vendors would also need to break the ABI, which they avoid, so they choose to keep the slow but compatible layout.

libstdc++ ships two implementations of std::string and std::list side by side, selected by the macro _GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI (1 = new, 0 = old).

The new ABI is needed for C++11 conformance (for example, a std::string with small-buffer optimization and list::size() in O(1)). The two sets get different mangled names (the new ones sit in an inline namespace __cxx11), so old and new code can live in one program, but passing a string between a library built with 0 and your code built with 1 gives link errors.

It makes every symbol hidden by default, so only the ones you mark as exported are visible outside the shared library.

Benefits: a smaller dynamic symbol table, faster load, fewer symbol clashes between libraries, better inlining and dead-code removal, and a smaller ABI surface to keep stable. Mark the public API with __attribute__((visibility("default"))) or an export macro; everything else becomes free to change without breaking users.

code.title: Name mangling and extern "C"

followUps:
No, not safely: if a C++ exception propagates out of an extern "C" function into a caller that has no exception tables (C, Python ctypes, Rust FFI), the behavior is undefined and usually terminates the program.

The linkage only changes the symbol name, not how exceptions work. Catch everything at the boundary and translate it to an error code:

extern "C" int api_run() noexcept {
    try { run(); return 0; }
    catch (...) { return -1; }
}

Load the library with dlopen, look up an extern "C" factory function with dlsym, and call it through a function pointer.

void* h = dlopen("./plugin.so", RTLD_NOW);
using Make = Plugin* (*)();
auto make = (Make)dlsym(h, "create_plugin");
Plugin* p = make();   // later: destroy_plugin(p); dlclose(h);

The factory must be extern "C" so its symbol name is exactly create_plugin, not a mangled name. Also export a matching destroy function, and do not dlclose while objects from the plugin are alive.

code.title: Safe library boundary: opaque handle and caller buffer

followUps:
COM avoids the problem by making every object a pure abstract interface with a fixed binary layout, and by letting the object free itself.

The caller never calls new or delete on the object: it uses reference counting through AddRef and Release, and the object deletes itself inside its own module. Strings use BSTR with a shared allocator (SysAllocString/SysFreeString), so memory crosses the boundary with one agreed heap. Layout is a vtable of function pointers, which does not depend on the compiler.

Qt promises binary compatibility inside one major version: you can swap in a newer Qt 6.x .so without recompiling your program.

To keep that, Qt uses pimpl (d-pointers) so private data can change, never reorders or adds virtual functions in public classes, reserves spare slots, and adds new functionality as new non-virtual functions. It does not promise compatibility across major versions (Qt 5 to Qt 6) or across compilers with different ABIs.

code.title: Virtual destructor, unique_ptr and shared_ptr

followUps:
Because unique_ptr<Base> deletes through a plain Base*, while shared_ptr stores a deleter that was built when the pointer was created.

When you write shared_ptr<void> p = make_shared<Derived>(), the control block already holds a deleter that knows the real type Derived. Destroying p runs it, so ~Derived executes even though the pointer type is void. A unique_ptr<void> has no such memory and cannot delete properly by default.

When the class is meant to be a base for inheritance only and nobody should delete objects through a base pointer.

Example: CRTP mixins or policy classes like struct Counter<T>. A protected non-virtual destructor makes delete basePtr; a compile error, so the misuse is blocked, and you avoid the vptr and the virtual call overhead. Derived classes still destroy normally.

code.title: Copy elision, NRVO and implicit move with a Tracer

followUps:
A Tracer is a small class that prints from its constructor, copy, move and destructor, so you can see exactly which operations happen.

In the program above: return Pinned(); prints only the constructor (guaranteed elision). T x(1); return x; prints ctor and dtor (NRVO, typical). Two candidates prints ctor 2, ctor 3, move 2, dtor 3, dtor 2, dtor 2: one move, no copy. return std::move(x) forces one extra move. NRVO itself is optional, so the second and third outputs can vary between compilers.

Yes, in a limited way: throwing a local object may copy or move it, and that copy can be elided, but it is optional, not guaranteed.

throw T(); creates the exception object directly from the prvalue (C++17). The catch clause catch (T e) copies from the exception object; catch (const T& e) avoids that copy. For throw x; with a named local, the compiler may skip the copy, but the type must still be copyable or movable.

code.title: What does this print? static vs dynamic type

followUps:
Unspecified means the compiler may choose among several valid results, and the program is still correct; undefined means anything may happen.

Example: f(g(), h()). The order in which g and h are called is unspecified: either prints "gh" or "hg", and both are fine. In contrast, i = i++ + 1 in old C++ was undefined. Another unspecified case is the address order of separately allocated objects.

C++17 fixed the order of evaluation in several expressions, while function arguments are still unordered.

Now guaranteed: a << b and a >> b evaluate left to right, a = b evaluates right side first, a[b] evaluates a first, a.b() evaluates a first, and &&, ||, ,, ?: already were ordered. So cout << f() << g(); always calls f first. Arguments to a function are still evaluated in any order (but not interleaved).

code.title: variant + visit versus virtual functions

followUps:
The expression problem is the difficulty of extending a design in two directions at once: adding new types and adding new operations, without editing existing code.

With virtual functions, a new type is easy (a new subclass) but a new operation means editing every class. With std::variant and visit, a new operation is easy (a new visitor) but a new type means editing the variant and all visitors. Example: 5 shapes and 3 operations is 15 cells; each approach makes one axis cheap and the other costly.

Give the type-erased wrapper a small inline buffer and construct the callable there if it fits, otherwise allocate on the heap.

alignas(std::max_align_t) unsigned char buf[32];
if constexpr (sizeof(F) <= 32 && is_nothrow_move_constructible_v<F>)
    new (buf) Model<F>(std::move(f));   // inline
else ptr = new Model<F>(std::move(f));  // heap

You must remember which case is used so the destructor and moves behave correctly, and the model must be relocatable with a virtual move_to or function table. Small lambdas then never allocate.
